title: The Digital Hive and the End of a Common World
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/ethan-j-podell
text:
The 77,303,568 people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 were apparently unfazed by the more than 30,000 false or misleading statements he made during his first term, according to a Washington Post count. We don’t yet have the number for his second term, though the pattern of deception is much the same: endless and escalating nonsense about economic, foreign policy, health, and election topics. Even the White House website disputes Trump’s claim that in his second term he has attracted $21 trillion of investments in the United States. The White House number, also disputed, puts the figure at $11 trillion. 

Unaware may be more accurate than unfazed here. The two sources for that 30,000 figure, the Washington Post and CNN, reach relatively few voters. (The Washington Post’s 2026 circulation, print and digital, is approximately 2.6 million readers. CNN’s primetime viewership in August 2026 was 625,000. Some 152 million people voted in the 2024 presidential election.) Even the two leading, partisan cable news networks—MS NOW and Fox News—today reach only slightly more than one percent of our adult population. As for that $10 trillion discrepancy about new investments in the country, very few Americans (around 1.2 million per month) ever check the White House website. 

So where are most Americans getting their news? While the New York Times, CNN, and Fox News are the top three new sites in terms of monthly visits, when the Pew Research Center asked people what sources they regularly rely upon for news, around 40 percent of US adults said they rely on either Facebook or YouTube. In other words, more than 100 million American adults get their news from those two platforms. Recall that in the 2024 election, around 150 million people voted. 

Very little of the news on Facebook and YouTube resembles conventional journalism, which has formal editorial structures, standards, and accountability mechanisms. The New York Times, CNN, and (presumably) Fox News have fact-checkers, plus editorial reviews before publication. They also try to follow professional standards and conventions such as sourcing, verifying, and separating reporting from opinion. Institutional journalism has policies about correcting errors they have made. There’s a masthead, or its equivalent, with names and addresses you can use, for instance, in a defamation lawsuit. The New York Times has been around for 175 years. It’s not going anywhere. Advertiser pressure is another accountability force, since those revenues are essential to their business. (YouTube and Facebook rely on advertising and have been subject to advertiser pressure, but not in connection with their news feeds.)

News on YouTube is personality-driven content presented, for the most part, as commentary offered in short video clips. YouTube Shorts, formatted to be viewed on cellphones, are typically fifteen to thirty seconds long. These shorts include a provocative claim, a dramatic soundbite, a reaction shot—or all three. The news is presented this way because YouTube, and its competitors, “measure success in seconds of dwell time, not seconds of deliberation.” Most of those clips are excerpts from a podcast, cable-news segment, or press conference that have been edited into a message focused on an angry exchange, a gotcha moment, or a one-liner. There’s no context connecting the clip to the underlying news event that occasioned the comment. 

Most Meta news posts—Facebook Reels that skew older as well as Instagram Reels targeting 18–34-year-olds—are similar opinion or reaction pieces. Much of that content, according to Pew Research, is posted by influencers, who are not journalists. Around 20–25 percent of Americans adults, or 55 million people, are getting their news from commentary about current events, much of which comes in the form of a meme or hot take rather than a link to a story. 

Moreover, because most of this news is pre-filtered by friends and family in a user’s network of contacts, it is just another person’s earlier reaction to an event. The Pew Research Center calculated that 85 percent of Facebook users who regularly get their news on that site are receiving it from family and friends. They’re also receiving it, perhaps indirectly, from journalists, advocacy groups and influencers. Fifty-eight percent, according to Pew, said they had no idea what the source of their news was.

In response to my recent search on Facebook for “today’s important news,” the first piece offered was commentary from Dan Bongino, a political influencer with some five million followers. This news story was a fifteen-second clip of Bongino celebrating Trump for denigrating James Talarico because he’s a vegetarian. Using his stock vulgarity, Trump said that Talarico’s campaign for the Senate is all about “beating meat.” 

The Washington Post’s report about Trump’s 30,000 false or misleading statements was some 2,000 words. A typical fifteen-second Facebook Reel or YouTube Short will have 30 words; a sixty-second commentary or influencer piece will have no more than 150. Informing the audience is not the objective. In contrast, as a long-time editor at the New York Times put it recently, “the main thing that motivates anyone in my kind of job is the desire to inform readers and get them the truth—as soon as possible and with as much explanation and nuance as possible. It’s a mission.”

By presenting most of the news as a free-for-all of user feedback and opinion-spouting, with little explanation or nuance, social media has upended the idea that journalistic sources create and disseminate the news to the audience. Digital platforms promote the news as a beehive of commentary to an audience of bees. In credible journalism, the hive is not the metaphor: What it offers is a lighthouse, a beam of light.

Persuasion and Rhetoric

Research on how persuasion works explains that while the hive hums with energy, none of it goes to engaging  with discourse or dialogue. Persuasion happens along two pathways. according to Richard E. Petty and John T. Cacioppo in their 1986 paper “The Elaboration Likelihood Model of Persuasion.” The “central route” requires thoughtful consideration of the merits of the information presented and relies on evidence and logical analysis. The “peripheral route” emphasizes surface cues: how confident the speaker sounds; how simple and repetitive the message is; whether the speaker seems to be “one of us”; and how much emotional arousal the message generates. Audiences default to peripheral processing when they are not motivated to scrutinize an argument, because they are unwilling to make the effort to delve into or corroboratee a claim. It’s evident that peripheral processing is how the news is consumed on social media. 

Compounding the problem, according to Emma L. Henderson and fellow researchers in their study, “The Trajectory of Truth: A Longitudinal Study of the Illusory Truth Effect,” is the “illusory truth effect,” in which repeated statements, accurate or not, are perceived as more true than novel ones because repetition increases “processing fluency”--the ease with which a claim is processed unconsciously. Previous presidents, of course, used slogans, and every slogan needs to be repeated, but none of them were as hooked on repetitive sloganeering as Trump clearly  is. Biden had one signature slogan about his infrastructure plans for the first two years of his presidency: “Build Back Better.” Trump has a saddlebag full of slogans—MAGA, “drain the swamp,” “drill, baby, drill,” “witch hunt,” “fake news,” “many people are saying”—that have regularly been recycled in his posts, press interactions, and speeches.

A 2024 study of presidential speech going back to 1961 found “considerable evidence that Trump’s speech patterns diverge from those of all major party nominees for the presidency in recent history…[notably, his] employment of divisive and antagonistic language, particularly when targeting his political opponents.” Divisiveness is defined “as language intended to impugn the speaker’s target by attacking their intelligence, integrity, or intentions.… More than just impolite or insulting, divisive speech…is explicitly intended to serve the political purposes of delegitimization and marginalization.” No other president has ever used words such as “stupid,” “crazy,” “corrupt,” “dishonest,” “disgrace,” “incompetent,” or “ridiculous” with anything approaching Trump’s frequency. Indeed, previous presidents almost never used such language in public address.

Trump’s divisive speech, the fifth-grade grammar, the adolescent fixation on crude language, and the simplistic diction all align with what users expect from the news on social media. The cruder and more outrageous the language, the greater the number of comments and reactions, and the greater the user social engagement, which is the financial engine driving all digital platforms. (Bongino calling Trump the GOAT—the Greatest of All Time—is big business, earning him an estimated $8 million a year from advertising on his podcasts and radio shows, as is his stake in the company distributing his videos, worth several hundred million dollars.) 

The algorithms that run all this calculate the probability that if you clicked on a Dan Bongino clip, you’ll likely want to watch Y, a clip from another commentator spouting the same stuff. And if you watched most of Y, you’ll next be offered Z. This echo chamber, this “dwelling” on Facebook and YouTube, also exposes users to a slew of advertising on their screens, which taken together with Bongino-type posts is both addictive and exhausting. It’s not surprising that digital bees are unwilling to scrutinize, or delve into a claim. Dwelling is a much easier assignment than delving. 

Trumpspeak updates historian Richard Hofstadter’s characterization of the paranoid style in American politics. That heated and exaggerated rhetorical style insists there are hidden, malevolent forces doing serious damage to the country and its values. Hofstadter described the history of this rhetoric in fringe movements, such as nineteenth-century Protestant nativism and McCarthyism. Trump has brought that style from the fringe and into the Oval Office. He’s used that style five times more frequently than the historical political norm, according to Roderick P. Hart in his “Donald Trump and the Return of the Paranoid Style.” As early as 2018, Trump called mainstream media “an enemy of the people,” a phrase used by Lenin and Stalin to designate political prisoners and dissidents marked for elimination. (Joseph McCarthy’s red-baiting slogan, “the enemy within,” was relatively mild in comparison.) 

Trump is a master of rhetoric. This is unsurprising because every successful demagogue must be facile at using persuasive language, usually in a highly weaponized form. In addition to ad hominem (“Crooked Hillary”) and ad baculum (which seeks compliance through intimidation, as in “agree with me or something bad will happen,”), there is his frequent use of ad populum rhetoric: “Many people have said…or believe.…” The last ploy invokes an imaginary popular chorus as proof of a claim, but it is evidence-free rhetoric, since we never learn anything about who those “many people” are. Nasty and exaggerated speech is the lingua franca of news on the hive.

There’s a distinction between lying and bullshit, as Harry G. Frankfurt noted in his influential 2005 book On Bullshit. The liar knows what’s true but deliberately conceals it, whereas the bullshitter has no interest at all in that distinction. Political lying entails what Hannah Arendt called “defactualization” in which rhetoric is used to make a claim bearing no relation to factual truth. It seeks to replace reality entirely, not merely obscure it. Political lying attacks the very possibility of what Arendt called a shared “common world,” where opinions will vary but are tethered to a common understanding of what constitutes the facts. If political lying can simply fabricate the facts, there’s no common world for opinions to be about. 

The bullshitter operates differently. His goal is to impress an audience, and like the stage actor he resembles, much of what he says is completely improvised. But unlike an actor who must work to learn his lines, the bullshitter can say whatever he wants, or needs, to make that impression. 

Whether Trump is best described as a liar or a bullshitter is a close call. Perhaps he’s both. Who’s to say that you can’t shift easily from one to the other? There’s ample evidence for both in his obliviousness to the truth and his wanton disregard of it. 

And most of us, for various reasons, seem willing to let him get away with it. 

A Nation of Sloppy Thinkers

All this has destabilized our democracy, and the problem here is more extensive than what is captured in the warning that an informed citizenry is a bedrock requirement for a functioning republic. Social media has turned us into a nation of sloppy thinkers, where sharing or liking a Dan Bongino post is as deep as thought gets. Equality in America, as Alexis de Tocqueville observed, did not lead us to trust our own thinking, to become independent-minded, but made us reliant on what we now call groupthink. “In times of equality men have no faith in one another…but an almost unlimited trust in the judgment of the public,” Tocqueville wrote in Democracy in America, “for it does not seem plausible to them that when all have the same enlightenment, truth is not found on the side of the greatest number.… [The public] does not persuade [one] of its beliefs. It imposes them and makes them penetrate souls by a sort of immense pressure of the minds of all upon the intellect of each.”

In other words, it’s all about the numbers, the metrics. Truth anchored in the facts is replaced by what most people think is true. Tocqueville worried about the omnipotence of the majority and the risk of tyranny that might follow from it. We should too. Two-thirds of the people who voted in 2024 got their news from the digital hive. 

That the digital hive is conducive to liars and bullshitters is, of course, a consequence and not the cause of why so many people today distrust traditional journalism and fact-based reality. That distrust came about because many Americans don’t believe traditional media present the news fully, fairly and accurately. The many failings and shortcomings of traditional media have been widely documented and discussed, including by the traditional media outlets themselves (a self-monitoring completely absent in the hive media). Not surprisingly, according to a 2025 Gallup poll, only 28 percent of Americans trust mass media a “great deal of the time,” in stark contrast to the 70 percent who said they did in the 1970s. 

One  reason 70 percent of Americans trusted mass media back then is that there were no alternative sources for national news. When Walter Cronkite of CBS signed off each weeknight with “And that’s the way it is,” viewers believed him because they got more or less the same version of the news if they watched the only other alternatives: John Chancellor on NBC, Harry Reasoner on ABC, or Robert MacNeil on PBS. Cronkite unquestionably enjoyed a special connection and popularity with viewers. A 1972 poll reported that  people believed he was the most trusted man in America. 

As the news oligopoly lost power and was eventually replaced by a horde of outlets, audience, trust did not disappear but underwent a realignment. People who rely on Newsmax, Breitbart, and One America News Network today trust those sources, just as they distrust the New York Times and CNN. 

It s also been said that trust eroded because many major news organizations either missed, ignored, or buried coverage of some important events, such as the COVID lab-leak story, the lead-up to the 2008 financial crisis, and Joe Biden’s age-related decline. 

Moreover, there’s the belief that traditional American journalism has become elitist, serving affluent, well-educated liberals while ignoring issues and concerns of working people and the middle class. Alienated by the mainstream media, Americans have turned to the digital hive. The finances of journalism have also played a role in this class divide, as traditional media owners realized that advertisers would pay a premium to reach an affluent audience. For that business model to work, the editorial side would need to favor coverage which aligned with the largely progressive views and news expectations of that college-educated audience. 

As significant amounts of advertising revenue moved to YouTube and Facebook, many local newspapers closed. That’s significant because local news has consistently been seen as more trustworthy and less partisan than national news. Northwestern University tracks what it calls the “news desert,” counties with no local news source at all. As of 2025, roughly 50 million Americans live in counties with limited or no local news. Nearly 40 percent of all US local newspapers have disappeared since 2005. As local news disappears, people are increasingly turning to the hive for all that passes as the news. 

It’s been twenty-five years since Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone highlighted the collapse in social trust that coincided with Americans losing connections to civic life. Among his findings were that people who regularly read a daily newspaper had more engagement with community life. Today, fewer than 10 percent of American regularly read a newspaper and only 25 percent read news websites or apps. Local papers, along with churches, clubs (and bowling leagues), served as crucial  mediating institutions, standing between the individual and the megastructures of public life, translating complexities such as governmental action into understandable narratives. By curating a common set of facts, local news helped establish a baseline of reality for the whole of society. 

Without that baseline, social integration weakens or disappears, distrust fosters distemper, fusing with greater cynicism and an openness to conspiracy theories. With the mediator missing, the news becomes spectacle: a 24/7 stream of dramatic, disconnected segments performed for audiences who can’t stop watching them, even though they explain little, if anything.
